name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q01 - Organisms excluded from Kingdom Plantae

questiontext.text: Under the modern understanding of Whittaker's Five Kingdom classification, which of the following organisms earlier placed in Plantae are now excluded from Kingdom Plantae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Under Whittaker's (1969) Five Kingdom classification, living organisms are grouped into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Animalia, and Plantae.

Step 2: Evaluation of Excluded Groups
Fungi, as well as members of Monera and Protista that possess cell walls, have been excluded from Plantae even though earlier classifications placed them there. Consequently, cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are no longer classified under algae or Plantae.

Step 3: Final Answer
Fungi and cell-walled members of Monera and Protista (including cyanobacteria) are excluded from Kingdom Plantae.

answer.text: Bryophytes and pteridophytes
Fungi, and cell-walled members of Monera and Protista
Chlorophyceae and Rhodophyceae
Gymnosperms and monocotyledons

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q02 - Basis of artificial classification system

questiontext.text: The artificial system of classification proposed by Linnaeus was primarily based on which of the following?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earliest classification systems were artificial and relied on only a few gross superficial morphological characters such as habit, colour, number, and shape of leaves.

Step 2: Linnaeus's System
Specifically, the artificial system given by Linnaeus was based mainly on vegetative characters or on the androecium structure.

Step 3: Final Answer
Linnaeus's artificial classification system was based mainly on vegetative characters or androecium structure.

answer.text: Evolutionary relationships and common ancestry
Ultrastructure, anatomy, and embryology
Chromosome number and behaviour
Vegetative characters or the androecium structure

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q03 - Major pigments in green algae

questiontext.text: Members of Chlorophyceae (green algae) are usually grass green in colour due to the dominance of which pigments?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Algae are classified into three main classes largely based on the type of pigments they possess and their stored food.

Step 2: Pigments in Chlorophyceae
Members of Chlorophyceae are grass green because of the dominance of chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, which are localised in definite chloroplasts. In contrast, Phaeophyceae possess chlorophyll a, c, and fucoxanthin, while Rhodophyceae possess chlorophyll a, d, and r-phycoerythrin.

Step 3: Final Answer
Chlorophyll a and b are the dominant pigments in Chlorophyceae.

answer.text: Chlorophyll a and b
Chlorophyll a, c, and fucoxanthin
Chlorophyll a, d, and phycoerythrin
Chlorophyll b and xanthophylls only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q04 - Stored food in Rhodophyceae

questiontext.text: In Rhodophyceae (red algae), food is stored in the form of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each algal class stores carbohydrates in a characteristic form.

Step 2: Comparison of Stored Food
Chlorophyceae store food as starch, and Phaeophyceae store complex carbohydrates as mannitol or laminarin. Rhodophyceae store food as floridean starch, which is structurally very similar to amylopectin and glycogen.

Step 3: Final Answer
Food in Rhodophyceae is stored as floridean starch.

answer.text: Laminarin and mannitol
Cellulose and algin
Floridean starch
Pectin and poly sulphate esters

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q05 - Bryophytes as amphibians of plant kingdom

questiontext.text: Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Habitat and Reproduction of Bryophytes
Bryophytes usually grow in damp, humid, and shaded localities on soil.

Step 2: Dependence on Water
Although they can live on soil, they require water for sexual reproduction because the male gametes (antherozoids) are released into water to reach and fertilise the egg in the archegonium.

Step 3: Final Answer
Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because they can live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction.

answer.text: They possess true roots, stems, and leaves adapted to both land and water
They can live in soil but are dependent on water for sexual reproduction
They reproduce exclusively by zoospores in aquatic habitats
Their sporophyte is free-living and aquatic

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q06 - First terrestrial plants with vascular tissues

questiontext.text: Evolutionarily, which group represents the first terrestrial plants to possess well-differentiated vascular tissues (xylem and phloem)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evolutionary Progression
Algae are largely aquatic and thalloid, while bryophytes lack true roots, stems, leaves, and vascular tissues.

Step 2: Vascularisation in Pteridophytes
Pteridophytes (including horsetails and ferns) are evolutionarily the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues—xylem and phloem—along with true roots, stems, and leaves.

Step 3: Final Answer
Pteridophytes are the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues.

answer.text: Pteridophytes
Bryophytes
Gymnosperms
Rhodophyceae

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q07 - Characteristic of gymnosperm ovules and seeds

questiontext.text: Gymnosperms are referred to as naked-seeded plants because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Etymology and Structure
The term gymnosperm is derived from gymnos (naked) and sperma (seeds).

Step 2: Ovule and Seed Exposure
In gymnosperms, the ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and remain exposed both before and after fertilisation. Consequently, the seeds that develop post-fertilisation are not covered by a fruit wall.

Step 3: Final Answer
Gymnosperms are naked-seeded because their ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and remain exposed before and after fertilisation.

answer.text: Their seeds lack a seed coat
They do not produce ovules
Their seeds are enclosed within a fleshy fruit
Their ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and remain exposed

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q08 - Tallest gymnosperm tree species

questiontext.text: Which of the following gymnosperms is the giant redwood tree, known to be one of the tallest tree species?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Growth Habit of Gymnosperms
Gymnosperms include medium-sized trees, tall trees, and shrubs.

Step 2: Identification of Tallest Species
Among gymnosperms, the giant redwood tree Sequoia is one of the tallest tree species in the plant kingdom.

Step 3: Final Answer
Sequoia is the giant redwood tree species among gymnosperms.

answer.text: Cycas
Ginkgo
Sequoia
Cedrus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q09 - Characteristics of monocotyledons

questiontext.text: Which set of characters accurately describes monocotyledonous angiosperms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Angiosperms
Angiosperms are divided into two classes: dicotyledons and monocotyledons.

Step 2: Features of Monocotyledons
Monocotyledons are characterised by seeds having a single cotyledon, parallel venation in leaves, and trimerous flowers (having three members in each floral whorl). Dicotyledons, on the other hand, have two cotyledons, reticulate venation, and tetramerous or pentamerous flowers.

Step 3: Final Answer
Monocotyledons are characterised by single-cotyledonous seeds, parallel venation, and trimerous flowers.

answer.text: Two cotyledons, reticulate venation, pentamerous flowers
Single cotyledon, parallel venation, trimerous flowers
Single cotyledon, reticulate venation, tetramerous flowers
Two cotyledons, parallel venation, trimerous flowers

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q10 - Dominant phase in haplontic life cycle

questiontext.text: In a haplontic life cycle, the dominant, photosynthetic, free-living phase is the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a haplontic life cycle, the sporophytic generation is represented only by the one-celled diploid zygote, and there are no free-living sporophytes.

Step 2: Dominant Phase
Meiosis in the zygote produces haploid spores that divide mitotically to form the haploid gametophyte, which is the dominant, photosynthetic, free-living phase (e.g., Volvox, Spirogyra).

Step 3: Final Answer
The dominant, photosynthetic, free-living phase in a haplontic life cycle is the haploid gametophyte.

answer.text: Haploid gametophyte
Diploid sporophyte
Multicellular zygote
Triploid endosperm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q11 - Natural classification system features and proponents

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the natural classification system for flowering plants given by George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Natural classification systems were developed to overcome the limitations of artificial systems by focusing on natural affinities among organisms.

Step 2: Features Considered
Unlike artificial systems that used only gross superficial morphological characters, natural classification systems consider not only external features but also internal features such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology, and phytochemistry.

Step 3: Final Answer
The natural classification system given by Bentham and Hooker considers both external features and internal features like ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology, and phytochemistry.

answer.text: It relies exclusively on chromosome number, structure, and behaviour
It gives equal weightage only to vegetative characters and floral colour
It considers both external features and internal features such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology, and phytochemistry
It uses computers to assign numbers and codes to hundreds of observable characters simultaneously

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q12 - Numerical taxonomy cytotaxonomy and chemotaxonomy

questiontext.text: When there is no supporting fossil evidence, taxonomists resolve difficulties in classification using modern tools. Which tool is based on cytological information such as chromosome number, structure, and behaviour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Distinction Between Modern Taxonomic Tools
Numerical taxonomy uses computers to process all observable characters by assigning numbers and codes so that each character gets equal importance. Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of plants to resolve confusions.

Step 2: Definition of Cytotaxonomy
Cytotaxonomy is specifically based on cytological information such as chromosome number, structure, and behaviour.

Step 3: Final Answer
Cytotaxonomy is based on chromosome number, structure, and behaviour.

answer.text: Numerical taxonomy
Chemotaxonomy
Artificial taxonomy
Cytotaxonomy

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q13 - Habitats and associations of algae

questiontext.text: Algae are largely aquatic, but some species also occur in association with fungi and animals. Which of the following correctly represents these associations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Algal Habitats
Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic, and largely aquatic (freshwater and marine) organisms, though they also occur on moist stones, soils, and wood.

Step 2: Symbiotic and Epizoic Associations
Some algae occur in symbiotic association with fungi as lichens, and some occur on animals, such as on the sloth bear.

Step 3: Final Answer
Algae occur in association with fungi in lichens and with animals such as on the sloth bear.

answer.text: Lichens (with fungi) and on sloth bear (with animals)
Mycorrhiza (with fungi) and coralloid roots (with cyanobacteria)
Prothallus (with fungi) and gemma cups (with animals)
Peat (with fungi) and holdfast (with animals)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q14 - Sexual reproduction types in algae

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of algae and their mode of sexual reproduction is correctly matched?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Types of Sexual Reproduction in Algae
Isogamous reproduction involves fusion of two gametes similar in size, which may be flagellated (as in Ulothrix) or non-flagellated (as in Spirogyra). Anisogamous reproduction involves fusion of two gametes dissimilar in size, as seen in species of Eudorina. Oogamous reproduction involves fusion between one large, non-motile female gamete and a smaller, motile male gamete, as seen in Volvox and Fucus.

Step 2: Evaluation
Therefore, Spirogyra exhibits isogamous reproduction with non-flagellated (non-motile) gametes.

Step 3: Final Answer
Spirogyra – Isogamous with non-flagellated gametes is correctly matched.

answer.text: Eudorina – Oogamous
Spirogyra – Isogamous with non-flagellated gametes
Ulothrix – Anisogamous
Volvox – Isogamous with flagellated gametes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q15 - Hydrocolloids from marine algae

questiontext.text: Certain marine brown and red algae produce large amounts of commercially useful hydrocolloids (water-holding substances). Identify the hydrocolloids obtained from brown algae and red algae, respectively.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrocolloids are water-holding substances produced commercially by specific marine algae.

Step 2: Identification of Sources
Marine brown algae (Phaeophyceae) produce algin, whereas marine red algae (Rhodophyceae) produce carrageen.

Step 3: Final Answer
Algin is obtained from brown algae and carrageen is obtained from red algae.

answer.text: Carrageen and algin
Agar and laminarin
Algin and carrageen
Mannitol and floridean starch

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q16 - Agar sources and Chlorella uses

questiontext.text: Agar, used to grow microbes and in the preparation of ice-creams and jellies, is obtained from:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Economic Importance of Algae
Algae provide several commercially important products such as food, hydrocolloids, agar, and protein supplements.

Step 2: Source of Agar
Agar is obtained from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria. In contrast, Chlorella is a unicellular green alga used as a protein-rich food supplement by space travellers, and Laminaria and Sargassum are brown algae used as food.

Step 3: Final Answer
Agar is obtained from Gelidium and Gracilaria.

answer.text: Chlorella and Spirulina
Laminaria and Sargassum
Ulothrix and Spirogyra
Gelidium and Gracilaria

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q17 - Pyrenoids and cell wall of Chlorophyceae

questiontext.text: Most members of Chlorophyceae have storage bodies called pyrenoids located in the chloroplasts, along with a rigid cell wall. What do pyrenoids and the two cell wall layers consist of?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Composition of Pyrenoids
In Chlorophyceae, pyrenoids are storage bodies located within chloroplasts. Pyrenoids contain protein besides starch.

Step 2: Cell Wall Structure
Green algae usually have a rigid cell wall made of an inner layer of cellulose and an outer layer of pectose.

Step 3: Final Answer
Pyrenoids contain protein besides starch, and the cell wall has an inner layer of cellulose and an outer layer of pectose.

answer.text: Pyrenoids contain protein besides starch; cell wall has inner cellulose and outer pectose
Pyrenoids contain mannitol besides lipids; cell wall has inner algin and outer cellulose
Pyrenoids contain floridean starch only; cell wall has inner pectin and outer cellulose
Pyrenoids contain laminarin besides protein; cell wall has inner pectose and outer cellulose

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q18 - Morphology and pigment variation in Phaeophyceae

questiontext.text: Members of Phaeophyceae vary in colour from olive green to various shades of brown depending upon the amount of which pigment, and their plant body is attached to the substratum by which structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pigment Responsible for Colour Variation
Brown algae possess chlorophyll a, c, carotenoids, and xanthophylls. Their colour varies from olive green to various shades of brown depending on the amount of the xanthophyll pigment fucoxanthin present in them.

Step 2: Plant Body Differentiation
The plant body of Phaeophyceae is usually attached to the substratum by a holdfast, has a stalk called the stipe, and a leaf-like photosynthetic organ called the frond.

Step 3: Final Answer
The colour depends on fucoxanthin, and attachment to the substratum is by a holdfast.

answer.text: r-phycoerythrin; rhizoids
Fucoxanthin; holdfast
Chlorophyll b; stipe
Fucoxanthin; frond

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q19 - Flagellar number and insertion across algal classes

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly represents the flagellar number and position of insertion in Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae, and Rhodophyceae, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Flagellar Features in Each Algal Class
In Chlorophyceae, flagella are 2–8 in number, equal in length, and apical in insertion. In Phaeophyceae, there are 2 unequal, laterally inserted flagella. In Rhodophyceae, flagella are completely absent.

Step 2: Final Answer
The flagellar number and insertion are 2–8, equal, apical in Chlorophyceae; 2, unequal, lateral in Phaeophyceae; and absent in Rhodophyceae.

answer.text: 2, unequal, lateral; 2–8, equal, apical; Absent
2–8, equal, lateral; 2, equal, apical; 2, unequal, lateral
2–8, equal, apical; 2, unequal, lateral; Absent
Absent; 2, unequal, apical; 2–8, equal, apical

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q20 - Cell wall and reproduction in Rhodophyceae

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding Rhodophyceae (red algae)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cell Wall Composition of Red Algae
The cell wall of Rhodophyceae consists of cellulose, pectin, and poly sulphate esters.

Step 2: Reproduction in Red Algae
Red algae reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation, asexually by non-motile spores, and sexually by non-motile gametes. Sexual reproduction is oogamous and accompanied by complex post-fertilisation developments.

Step 3: Final Answer
Rhodophyceae reproduce asexually by non-motile spores and sexually by non-motile gametes, with cell walls made of cellulose, pectin, and poly sulphate esters.

answer.text: They reproduce asexually by biflagellate pear-shaped zoospores
Sexual reproduction is isogamous with flagellated gametes
They are found exclusively in cold freshwater habitats
They reproduce asexually by non-motile spores and sexually by non-motile gametes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q21 - Sex organs and gametes in bryophytes

questiontext.text: In bryophytes, the sex organs are multicellular. Which of the following correctly describes the male and female sex organs and their gametes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Male Sex Organ in Bryophytes
The male sex organ is called the antheridium, and it produces biflagellate antherozoids (male gametes) that are released into water.

Step 2: Female Sex Organ in Bryophytes
The female sex organ is called the archegonium; it is flask-shaped and produces a single egg.

Step 3: Final Answer
The antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids, and the flask-shaped archegonium produces a single egg.

answer.text: Antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids; flask-shaped archegonium produces a single egg
Antheridium produces non-motile spermatia; archegonium produces four eggs
Archegonium produces multiflagellate antherozoids; antheridium produces a single egg
Both antheridium and archegonium are unicellular and produce motile gametes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q22 - Ecological and economic importance of mosses

questiontext.text: Which moss species provides peat used as fuel and as packing material for trans-shipment of living material due to its high water-holding capacity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ecological and Economic Roles of Mosses
Mosses along with lichens are the first organisms to colonise rocks and help prevent soil erosion by forming dense mats on soil.

Step 2: Specific Role of Sphagnum
Species of Sphagnum, a moss, provide peat that has long been used as fuel and as packing material for trans-shipment of living material because of its capacity to hold water.

Step 3: Final Answer
Sphagnum provides peat used as fuel and packing material.

answer.text: Funaria
Sphagnum
Marchantia
Polytrichum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q23 - Gemmae in liverworts

questiontext.text: In liverworts such as Marchantia, gemmae are specialised structures involved in asexual reproduction. Which of the following accurately describes gemmae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Asexual Reproduction in Liverworts
Asexual reproduction in liverworts takes place by fragmentation of thalli or by the formation of specialised structures called gemmae.

Step 2: Structure and Function of Gemmae
Gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds that develop in small receptacles called gemma cups located on the thalli. Once detached from the parent body, they germinate to form new individuals.

Step 3: Final Answer
Gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds formed in gemma cups on the thalli.

answer.text: Unicellular, non-green sexual spores produced inside the capsule
Diploid structures formed after fertilisation inside the archegonium
Green, multicellular, asexual buds developed in gemma cups on the thalli
Creeping, filamentous stages developed directly from haploid spores

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q24 - Protonema and leafy stage in mosses

questiontext.text: In mosses, the predominant gametophytic phase consists of two stages. How does the second stage (leafy stage) arise, and what are its characteristic features?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: First Stage of Moss Gametophyte
The first stage is the protonema stage, which develops directly from a spore and is creeping, green, branched, and frequently filamentous.

Step 2: Second Stage (Leafy Stage)
The second stage is the leafy stage, which develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud. It consists of upright, slender axes bearing spirally arranged leaves, attached to the soil through multicellular and branched rhizoids, and bears the sex organs.

Step 3: Final Answer
The leafy stage develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud and has upright axes with spirally arranged leaves and multicellular, branched rhizoids.

answer.text: It develops directly from the zygote and bears unicellular rhizoids
It develops from the capsule and has dorsiventral thalloid appendages
It develops directly from a spore as a creeping filamentous structure
It develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud and has upright axes with spirally arranged leaves and multicellular, branched rhizoids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q25 - Microphylls macrophylls and strobili in pteridophytes

questiontext.text: In pteridophytes, sporophylls may form distinct compact structures called strobili or cones. In which of the following pairs of genera are strobili or cones found?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Sporophylls and Strobili in Pteridophytes
In pteridophytes, the sporophytes bear sporangia subtended by leaf-like appendages called sporophylls.

Step 2: Genera Forming Strobili
In genera such as Selaginella and Equisetum, sporophylls form distinct compact structures called strobili or cones.

Step 3: Final Answer
Strobili or cones are found in Selaginella and Equisetum.

answer.text: Selaginella and Equisetum
Dryopteris and Pteris
Adiantum and Salvinia
Funaria and Sphagnum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q26 - Restricted spread of living pteridophytes

questiontext.text: Why is the spread of living pteridophytes limited and restricted to narrow geographical regions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Gametophyte (Prothallus) Requirements
In pteridophytes, spores germinate to give rise to inconspicuous, small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophytes called prothallus, which require cool, damp, shady places to grow.

Step 2: Water Requirement for Fertilisation
In addition to the specific habitat requirement of the prothallus, water is required for the transfer of antherozoids (male gametes) from the antheridia to the mouth of the archegonium.

Step 3: Final Answer
Their spread is limited because the gametophytes (prothallus) require cool, damp, shady places to grow and water is needed for fertilisation.

answer.text: They lack vascular tissues and true roots
Their gametophytes require cool, damp, shady places to grow and water is needed for fertilisation
Their sporophytes are completely dependent on the gametophyte for nutrition
They produce only non-motile spores that cannot be dispersed

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q27 - Heterospory in pteridophytes

questiontext.text: Genera like Selaginella and Salvinia produce two kinds of spores—macro (large) and micro (small) spores. This phenomenon is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Homospory vs Heterospory
In the majority of pteridophytes, all spores are of similar kinds; such plants are called homosporous.

Step 2: Definition of Heterospory
Genera such as Selaginella and Salvinia produce two kinds of spores—megaspores (macro) and microspores (micro)—and are known as heterosporous. This event is a precursor to the seed habit.

Step 3: Final Answer
The production of two kinds of spores (macro and micro) is known as heterospory.

answer.text: Homospory
Oogamy
Heterospory
Anisogamy

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q28 - Classes of Pteridophyta

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of pteridophyte genera belongs exclusively to the class Pteropsida?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Pteridophytes
Pteridophytes are divided into four classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).

Step 2: Evaluation of Sets
Only the group consisting of Dryopteris, Pteris, and Adiantum belongs entirely to Pteropsida.

Step 3: Final Answer
Dryopteris, Pteris, and Adiantum belong exclusively to Pteropsida.

answer.text: Selaginella, Lycopodium, Equisetum
Psilotum, Equisetum, Pteris
Selaginella, Dryopteris, Psilotum
Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q29 - Leaf adaptations in conifers

questiontext.text: In conifers (gymnosperms), how are the leaves adapted to reduce water loss and withstand extremes of temperature, humidity, and wind?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Leaf Adaptations in Gymnosperms
Leaves in gymnosperms are well-adapted to withstand extremes of temperature, humidity, and wind.

Step 2: Specific Xerophytic Features in Conifers
In conifers, the needle-like leaves reduce the surface area exposed to transpiration, while their thick cuticle and sunken stomata further help reduce water loss.

Step 3: Final Answer
Conifer leaves reduce water loss through needle-like leaves (reduced surface area), a thick cuticle, and sunken stomata.

answer.text: Needle-like leaves reducing surface area, thick cuticle, and sunken stomata
Broad, flat lamina with thin cuticle and raised stomata
Absence of stomata and presence of air bladders
Dorsiventral thalloid leaves covered with algin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q30 - Root associations in Pinus and Cycas

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the specialised root associations in Pinus and Cycas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Root Types in Gymnosperms
Gymnosperms generally possess tap roots, some of which form symbiotic associations.

Step 2: Specific Associations
In Pinus, roots have a fungal association in the form of mycorrhiza. In Cycas, small specialised roots called coralloid roots are associated with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

Step 3: Final Answer
Pinus has mycorrhiza (fungal association), whereas Cycas has coralloid roots associated with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.

answer.text: Pinus has coralloid roots with cyanobacteria; Cycas has mycorrhiza with fungi
Pinus has mycorrhiza (fungal association); Cycas has coralloid roots with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria
Both Pinus and Cycas have rhizoids associated with green algae
Both Pinus and Cycas lack tap roots and form only adventitious roots

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q31 - Stems and cones in Pinus and Cycas

questiontext.text: How do Pinus and Cycas differ with respect to stem branching and the distribution of male and female cones or sporophylls?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stem Branching
In gymnosperms, stems are unbranched in Cycas, whereas they are branched in Pinus and Cedrus.

Step 2: Distribution of Cones/Sporophylls
In Pinus, male and female cones or strobili may be borne on the same tree. However, in Cycas, male cones and megasporophylls are borne on different trees.

Step 3: Final Answer
Pinus has branched stems with male and female cones on the same tree, whereas Cycas has unbranched stems with male cones and megasporophylls on different trees.

answer.text: Pinus has unbranched stems with cones on different trees; Cycas has branched stems with cones on the same tree
Both Pinus and Cycas have branched stems and bear cones on the same tree
Pinus has branched stems with male and female cones on the same tree; Cycas has unbranched stems with male cones and megasporophylls on different trees
Both Pinus and Cycas have unbranched stems and bear cones on different trees

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q32 - Structure of angiosperm embryo sac

questiontext.text: In an angiosperm ovule, the female gametophyte (embryo sac) consists of which of the following cells and nuclei before fertilisation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formation of Embryo Sac
Inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores. Three degenerate and one divides to form the embryo sac.

Step 2: Cellular Organisation of Embryo Sac
Each embryo sac has a three-celled egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids), three antipodal cells, and two polar nuclei (which eventually fuse to form a diploid secondary nucleus).

Step 3: Final Answer
The embryo sac consists of a three-celled egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids), three antipodal cells, and two polar nuclei.

answer.text: Two egg cells, one synergid, two antipodals, and three polar nuclei
One egg cell, three synergids, two antipodals, and one polar nucleus
Two or more archegonia embedded in the nucellus
A three-celled egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids), three antipodal cells, and two polar nuclei

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q33 - Double fertilisation in angiosperms

questiontext.text: Double fertilisation, an event unique to angiosperms, involves which two fusions inside the embryo sac?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Discharge of Male Gametes
After pollination and pollen tube growth through the stigma and style, the pollen tube enters the embryo sac and discharges two male gametes.

Step 2: The Two Fusions
One male gamete fuses with the egg cell (syngamy) to form a diploid zygote. The other male gamete fuses with the diploid secondary nucleus (triple fusion) to produce the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

Step 3: Final Answer
Double fertilisation involves syngamy (male gamete + egg cell) and triple fusion (male gamete + diploid secondary nucleus).

answer.text: Syngamy (male gamete + egg cell) and triple fusion (male gamete + diploid secondary nucleus)
Fusion of two male gametes with two synergids
Fusion of one male gamete with an antipodal cell and another with the egg cell
Fusion of two polar nuclei with each other and fusion of two synergids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q34 - Haplo-diplontic life cycle in bryophytes vs pteridophytes

questiontext.text: Both bryophytes and pteridophytes exhibit a haplo-diplontic life cycle in which both phases are multicellular. How do they differ in their dominant phase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Haplo-diplontic Pattern in Bryophytes
In all bryophytes, the dominant, independent, photosynthetic phase is the haploid gametophyte, which alternates with a short-lived multicellular sporophyte that is totally or partially dependent on the gametophyte for anchorage and nutrition.

Step 2: Haplo-diplontic Pattern in Pteridophytes
In all pteridophytes, the diploid sporophyte is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic, vascular plant body, and it alternates with a multicellular, independent, short-lived haploid gametophyte.

Step 3: Final Answer
Bryophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte, whereas pteridophytes have a dominant diploid sporophyte.

answer.text: Bryophytes have a dominant diploid sporophyte; pteridophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte
Bryophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte; pteridophytes have a dominant diploid sporophyte
Both have a dominant diploid sporophyte, but bryophytes lack a multicellular gametophyte
Both have a dominant haploid gametophyte, but pteridophytes have a one-celled zygote as sporophyte

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q35 - Limitations of artificial classification system

questiontext.text: Why are artificial systems of classification considered unacceptable in modern plant taxonomy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nature of Artificial Systems
Artificial systems were based on a few gross superficial morphological characters or androecium structure, which often separated closely related species.

Step 2: Major Drawback Regarding Weightage
Furthermore, artificial systems gave equal weightage to vegetative and sexual characteristics. This is unacceptable because vegetative characters are more easily affected by the environment than sexual characters.

Step 3: Final Answer
Artificial systems separated closely related species and gave equal weightage to vegetative and sexual characters, even though vegetative characters are more easily affected by the environment.

answer.text: They rely only on fossil records and ignore living plants
They consider too many internal anatomical and phytochemical characters
They separated closely related species and gave equal weightage to vegetative and sexual characters, even though vegetative characters are easily affected by the environment
They group organisms strictly by evolutionary common ancestry

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q36 - Ecological role of algae and depth distribution of red algae

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately reflects the ecological significance of algae and the habitat distribution of Rhodophyceae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Global Ecological Role of Algae
At least half of the total carbon dioxide fixation on earth is carried out by algae through photosynthesis, increasing dissolved oxygen in their immediate environment and serving as primary producers for aquatic food cycles.

Step 2: Distribution of Rhodophyceae
Majority of red algae are marine with greater concentrations in warmer areas. They occur both in well-lighted regions close to the surface of water and at great depths in oceans where relatively little light penetrates.

Step 3: Final Answer
Algae carry out at least half of total CO₂ fixation on earth, and red algae occur both near the surface and at great depths in oceans where little light penetrates.

answer.text: Algae carry out less than 10% of global CO₂ fixation, and red algae are restricted to shallow freshwater ponds
Algae decrease dissolved oxygen in water, and red algae occur only in polar oceans
Algae fix CO₂ only in terrestrial soils, and red algae cannot survive in deep oceans
Algae carry out at least half of total CO₂ fixation on earth, and red algae occur both near the surface and at great depths in oceans

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q37 - Zoospores and gametes in Phaeophyceae vs Rhodophyceae

questiontext.text: Compare the reproductive structures of Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae. Which statement is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Zoospores and Gametes in Phaeophyceae
In most brown algae (Phaeophyceae), asexual reproduction occurs via biflagellate zoospores that are pear-shaped (pyriform) and have two unequal laterally attached flagella. Their gametes are also pyriform and bear two laterally attached flagella, and union may occur in water or within the oogonium.

Step 2: Spores and Gametes in Rhodophyceae
In red algae (Rhodophyceae), both asexual spores and sexual gametes are non-motile because flagella are absent.

Step 3: Final Answer
Phaeophyceae produce pyriform zoospores and gametes with two laterally attached flagella, whereas Rhodophyceae produce non-motile spores and gametes.

answer.text: Phaeophyceae have pyriform zoospores and gametes with two laterally attached flagella, whereas Rhodophyceae have non-motile spores and gametes
Both Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae produce biflagellate zoospores with equal apical flagella
Phaeophyceae have non-motile gametes, whereas Rhodophyceae have pyriform biflagellate gametes
Both classes lack asexual spores and reproduce solely by fragmentation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q38 - Fate of zygote in bryophytes vs haplontic algae

questiontext.text: How does the immediate fate of the zygote in bryophytes differ from that in haplontic algae such as Spirogyra?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Zygote Fate in Haplontic Algae
In haplontic algae like Spirogyra and Volvox, the zygote represents the entire sporophytic generation and undergoes meiosis (reduction division) directly to form haploid spores without forming a multicellular sporophyte.

Step 2: Zygote Fate in Bryophytes
In bryophytes, zygotes do not undergo reduction division immediately. Instead, they divide mitotically to produce a multicellular diploid body called a sporophyte, which remains attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it before some cells undergo meiosis to form haploid spores.

Step 3: Final Answer
In bryophytes, the zygote does not undergo immediate meiosis and instead forms a multicellular sporophyte attached to the gametophyte, whereas in haplontic algae the zygote undergoes meiosis directly.

answer.text: In bryophytes, the zygote undergoes immediate meiosis, whereas in haplontic algae it forms a free-living sporophyte
In bryophytes, the zygote does not undergo immediate meiosis and instead forms a multicellular dependent sporophyte, whereas in haplontic algae the zygote undergoes meiosis directly
In both groups, the zygote develops into an independent vascular sporophyte
In bryophytes, the zygote is haploid, whereas in haplontic algae it is triploid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q39 - Comparison of liverworts and mosses

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly differentiates mosses from liverworts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Gametophyte Differences
Liverworts (e.g., Marchantia) generally have a dorsiventral thalloid plant body closely appressed to the substrate (or tiny leaf-like appendages in two rows), whereas mosses have a protonema stage and a leafy stage with upright, slender axes bearing spirally arranged leaves and multicellular, branched rhizoids.

Step 2: Sporophyte Differences
While both have a sporophyte differentiated into a foot, seta, and capsule, the sporophyte in mosses is more elaborate than that in liverworts, and mosses possess an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal.

Step 3: Final Answer
Mosses have a protonema stage, spirally arranged leaves on upright axes, and a more elaborate sporophyte with an elaborate spore dispersal mechanism compared to liverworts.

answer.text: Liverworts have an elaborate spore dispersal mechanism, while mosses lack a capsule
Mosses have dorsiventral thalli with gemma cups, while liverworts have a protonema stage
Mosses have a protonema stage, spirally arranged leaves on upright axes, and a more elaborate sporophyte with elaborate spore dispersal
Liverworts have true vascular tissues, while mosses lack rhizoids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q40 - Precursor to seed habit in heterosporous pteridophytes

questiontext.text: Which evolutionary event in heterosporous pteridophytes (such as Selaginella and Salvinia) is considered a precursor to the seed habit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heterospory and Gametophyte Retention
In heterosporous pteridophytes, megaspores and microspores germinate to give rise to female and male gametophytes, respectively. Unlike homosporous pteridophytes, the female gametophytes in these heterosporous plants are retained on the parent sporophytes for variable periods.

Step 2: Embryo Development
The development of the zygotes into young embryos takes place within the female gametophytes while retained on the parent sporophyte. This event is considered an important evolutionary step and a precursor to the seed habit.

Step 3: Final Answer
Retention of the female gametophyte on the parent sporophyte and development of the zygote into a young embryo within it is the precursor to the seed habit.

answer.text: Formation of free-living photosynthetic prothallus in cool, damp soil
Development of compact strobili on homosporous sporophytes
Presence of vascular tissues in true roots and stems
Retention of the female gametophyte on the parent sporophyte and development of the zygote into a young embryo within it

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q41 - Gametophytes in gymnosperms

questiontext.text: Unlike bryophytes and pteridophytes, how do the male and female gametophytes behave in gymnosperms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Comparison with Bryophytes and Pteridophytes
In bryophytes, the gametophyte is the dominant free-living phase, and in pteridophytes, the gametophyte (prothallus) is an independent, free-living structure.

Step 2: Condition in Gymnosperms
In gymnosperms, the male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence. They remain within the sporangia retained on the sporophytes: the reduced male gametophyte is the pollen grain developed within microsporangia, and the multicellular female gametophyte bearing archegonia is retained within the megasporangium.

Step 3: Final Answer
In gymnosperms, the male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence and remain within sporangia retained on the sporophytes.

answer.text: They do not have an independent free-living existence and remain within the sporangia retained on the sporophytes
Both are free-living, photosynthetic, and independent of the sporophyte
Only the female gametophyte is free-living, while the male gametophyte is absent
They require external water for the swimming of antherozoids to the ovule

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q42 - Megasporangium and female gametophyte in gymnosperms

questiontext.text: In gymnosperms, how does the female gametophyte develop inside the ovule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structure of Gymnosperm Ovule
The megaspore mother cell is differentiated from one of the cells of the nucellus, which is protected by envelopes to form the composite structure called an ovule.

Step 2: Meiosis and Female Gametophyte Development
The megaspore mother cell divides meiotically to form four megaspores. One of the megaspores enclosed within the megasporangium develops into a multicellular female gametophyte that bears two or more archegonia (female sex organs).

Step 3: Final Answer
The megaspore mother cell divides meiotically to form four megaspores, and one enclosed megaspore develops into a multicellular female gametophyte bearing two or more archegonia.

answer.text: All four megaspores fuse to form a single seven-celled embryo sac
The megaspore mother cell divides meiotically into four megaspores, and one develops into a multicellular female gametophyte bearing two or more archegonia
The nucellus undergoes mitosis directly to form a diploid female gametophyte without meiosis
The female gametophyte develops outside the ovule on the soil as a prothallus

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q43 - Ploidy of various plant structures

questiontext.text: What is the correct ploidy sequence of: (i) protonemal cell of a moss, (ii) primary endosperm nucleus in a dicot, (iii) prothallus cell of a fern, and (iv) zygote of a fern?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ploidy of Moss and Fern Gametophyte Cells
The protonemal cell of a moss develops from a haploid spore and is part of the gametophyte, so it is haploid (n). The prothallus of a fern is the haploid gametophyte, so its cell is also haploid (n).

Step 2: Ploidy of Dicot PEN and Fern Zygote
The primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) in a dicot is formed by triple fusion (a haploid male gamete fusing with a diploid secondary nucleus), so it is triploid (3n). The zygote of a fern is formed by the fusion of a haploid male gamete and a haploid egg, so it is diploid (2n).

Step 3: Final Answer
The ploidy sequence is n, 3n, n, 2n.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q44 - Post-fertilisation events in angiosperms

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the post-fertilisation changes in an angiosperm flower?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fate of Embryo Sac Cells
After double fertilisation, the zygote develops into an embryo (with one or two cotyledons), and the primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) develops into endosperm that nourishes the developing embryo. The synergids and antipodals degenerate after fertilisation.

Step 2: Fate of Ovule and Ovary
During these post-fertilisation events, the ovules develop into seeds and the ovaries develop into fruit.

Step 3: Final Answer
Synergids and antipodals degenerate, PEN forms endosperm, ovules develop into seeds, and ovaries develop into fruit.

answer.text: Synergids form the seed coat, antipodals form the endosperm, and the ovary degenerates
Ovules develop into fruit, ovaries develop into seeds, and PEN degenerates
Antipodals develop into the embryo, and synergids nourish the endosperm
Synergids and antipodals degenerate, PEN forms endosperm, ovules develop into seeds, and ovaries develop into fruit

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q45 - Algal life cycle exceptions

questiontext.text: While most algal genera exhibit a haplontic life cycle, which of the following correctly identifies the exceptions that show haplo-diplontic and diplontic life cycles?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Typical Algal Pattern
Most algae, such as Volvox, Spirogyra, and some species of Chlamydomonas, follow a haplontic life cycle.

Step 2: Algal Exceptions
Some algal genera such as Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps exhibit a haplo-diplontic life cycle, whereas the brown alga Fucus exhibits a diplontic life cycle.

Step 3: Final Answer
Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps are haplo-diplontic, whereas Fucus is diplontic.

answer.text: Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps are haplo-diplontic; Fucus is diplontic
Volvox and Spirogyra are diplontic; Ectocarpus is haplontic
Fucus is haplo-diplontic; Polysiphonia and kelps are diplontic
All brown algae are strictly haplontic, while all red algae are diplontic

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q46 - Gametophytic phase across plant groups

questiontext.text: Considering the evolutionary trend of the gametophytic phase across plant groups, which statement is accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Gametophyte in Bryophytes and Pteridophytes
In bryophytes, the gametophyte is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic plant body. In pteridophytes, the gametophyte (prothallus) is still independent and multicellular, but it is inconspicuous and short-lived compared to the dominant vascular sporophyte.

Step 2: Gametophyte in Seed Plants
In seed-bearing plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms), which follow a diplontic life cycle, the diploid sporophyte is the dominant independent phase, and the gametophytic phase is highly reduced, represented by a single to few-celled (or limited-celled) structure retained on the sporophyte.

Step 3: Final Answer
The gametophyte shifts from being the dominant independent phase in bryophytes, to a small independent phase in pteridophytes, to a highly reduced dependent phase in gymnosperms and angiosperms.

answer.text: The gametophyte becomes progressively larger and more independent from bryophytes to angiosperms
The gametophyte shifts from the dominant independent phase in bryophytes, to a small independent phase in pteridophytes, to a highly reduced dependent phase in gymnosperms and angiosperms
Gymnosperms have a free-living photosynthetic gametophyte, whereas pteridophytes have a dependent gametophyte
Angiosperms lack a gametophytic phase completely

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q47 - Size range and distinguishing features of angiosperms

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about angiosperms is accurate regarding their size range and floral/seed characters?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Size Range of Angiosperms
Angiosperms range in size from the smallest flowering plant Wolffia to tall trees of Eucalyptus (over 100 metres).

Step 2: Dicot vs Monocot Characters
Dicotyledons have two cotyledons, reticulate venation in leaves, and tetramerous or pentamerous flowers, whereas monocotyledons have a single cotyledon, parallel venation, and trimerous flowers.

Step 3: Final Answer
Angiosperms range from Wolffia to Eucalyptus, and dicotyledons have two cotyledons, reticulate venation, and tetramerous or pentamerous flowers.

answer.text: They range from Sequoia to Chlorella, and dicots have trimerous flowers
Their seeds remain naked on megasporophylls, and monocots have reticulate venation
They range from Wolffia to Eucalyptus (over 100 m), and dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate venation, and tetramerous or pentamerous flowers
They lack double fertilisation and produce archegonia inside the ovary

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q48 - Site of meiosis across plant groups

questiontext.text: Where does reduction division (meiosis) take place in the life cycle of a moss, a fern, a gymnosperm, and an angiosperm?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Site of Meiosis in Bryophytes and Pteridophytes
In a moss (and liverwort), meiosis occurs in the spore mother cells inside the capsule of the sporophyte to produce haploid spores. In a fern (pteridophyte), meiosis occurs in the spore mother cells inside the sporangia borne on sporophylls.

Step 2: Site of Meiosis in Gymnosperms and Angiosperms
In a gymnosperm, meiosis occurs in the microspore mother cells inside microsporangia and in the megaspore mother cell inside the megasporangium (ovule). In an angiosperm, meiosis occurs in the pollen mother cells inside the anthers and in the megaspore mother cell inside the ovule.

Step 3: Final Answer
Meiosis occurs in the capsule of a moss, sporangia of a fern, microsporangia and megasporangia of a gymnosperm, and anthers and ovules of an angiosperm.

answer.text: Zygote in moss; prothallus in fern; pollen grain in gymnosperm; embryo sac in angiosperm
Protonema in moss; antheridium in fern; endosperm in gymnosperm; stigma in angiosperm
Archegonium in moss; rhizome in fern; archegonia in gymnosperm; synergids in angiosperm
Capsule in moss; sporangia in fern; microsporangia and megasporangia in gymnosperm; anthers and ovules in angiosperm
